source_batch.unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Documentary Letters of Credit

facts.statement: A bill of exchange under a credit is drawn by the beneficiary on the issuing bank, payable at the tenor in the credit, quoting the issuing bank's name and the credit number, in the currency of the credit and not exceeding its amount, with any correction authenticated by the drawer. A commercial invoice is made out by the beneficiary, normally in the name of the applicant, with goods described as in the credit, the order or contract number and credit number, and a value that does not exceed the credit amount; terms of sale such as FOB, C&F or CIF and shipping particulars are stated.

A bill of lading is a receipt from the shipowner or its agent that goods were shipped on a stated date on a named vessel. It should be a full set of negotiable originals as the credit requires; be signed by the shipowner or its authorised agent; describe the goods as in the credit and invoice; show the credit number and issuing bank; show whether freight is paid as the credit requires; be a "shipped on board" bill if the credit asks; be issued to the order of the shipper, blank endorsed or endorsed to the issuing bank as required; show a shipment date within the credit's period; indicate partial shipment or transhipment if permitted; and not be claused unless claused bills are permitted.

An insurance policy or certificate must be issued and signed by the insurance company or its agents; its date must be on or before the shipment date or it must show cover effective from the date of shipment; it must be in the currency of the credit and, unless the credit says otherwise, for 110% of the CIF or CIP value; it must show the voyage and the point where cover ends; claims must be payable in the applicant's country; it must be blank endorsed; and the goods description must match the credit. (The courseware cites UCP 500 article numbers for these points; in UCP 600 the insurance rules are in Article 28.)

A certificate of origin states the country of origin of the goods; it must be issued and signed by an independent authority such as a Chamber of Commerce and its details must be consistent with the other documents. Other documents such as the packing list, weight list, phytosanitary certificate and beneficiary's certificate must be made out as the credit requires and be consistent with each other and with the credit.

In every import, whatever the value remitted, the authorised dealer through which the remittance was made must ensure that the importer submits evidence of import: the bill of entry number, port code and date for marking evidence of import in IDPMS; or a customs assessment certificate or postal appraisal form for imports by post, or a courier bill of entry for imports by courier; or, for goods in a free trade warehousing zone, SEZ or bonded warehouse, the ex-bond bill of entry or similar document. For imports on delivery against acceptance, the bank verifies the evidence of import from IDPMS when remitting the bill; if the importer cannot produce it for genuine reasons such as non-arrival of the consignment or delay in customs clearance, the bank may allow reasonable time not exceeding three months from the date of remittance. The bank creates an Outward Remittance Message (ORM) for every such remittance.

RBI's Master Direction on Import of Goods and Services (updated 12 January 2026) is superseded, together with the Master Direction on Export of Goods and Services and the listed circulars, by RBI's Directions on Export and Import of Goods and Services of 16 January 2026, which come into force on 1 October 2026.

A bank receiving import bills directly from an overseas supplier must be fully satisfied about the importer's standing and track record and should obtain a report on each overseas supplier from the overseas banker or a reputed credit agency; the report need not be obtained where the invoice value does not exceed USD 300,000 and the bank is satisfied about the bona fides of the transaction and the importer.

The courseware advises banks, when opening credits for importers, to follow clear internal guidelines, exercise due diligence and know-your-customer rules, take extra care on large-value transactions or a sudden spurt in business, obtain a credit report on the overseas seller, be familiar with exchange control and trade control requirements, follow up evidence of imports, and for sight bills not retired to take possession of the goods and continue insurance. For usance credits the facility should go only to reputed clients with adequate security, because goods are delivered on acceptance.

Risks the courseware lists in credit transactions: rejection of documents for discrepancies, local law conflicting with the UCP, embargoes and currency restrictions, court stay orders stopping payment after acceptance, non-acceptance of documents until goods arrive, and disputes about quality after documents are accepted. Banks should open credits for regular customers, call for bills of lading in the name of the bank, avoid goods on the restricted list and obtain the import licence where required, and hedge large transactions by forward contract. Buyers should check the seller's creditworthiness and put safety clauses in the credit; sellers should prepare documents exactly as the credit requires.

The courseware states that for import bills under a credit the issuing bank, under FEDAI guidelines, may hold sight-bill documents for a number of days set by its own policy after receipt and, if the importer has not retired the bill, crystallise the foreign currency liability into rupees at the bill selling rate or the rate at which a forward contract was booked; usance bills are crystallised on the due date.

payload.title: The draft and the invoice: what a checker looks for
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Draft (bill of exchange)**
- drawn by the **beneficiary** on the **issuing bank**
- payable at the **tenor** the credit states (sight or a stated period)
- shows the **issuing bank's name** and the **credit number**
- in the **currency of the credit**, for an amount **not above** it
- any **correction** authenticated by the drawer

**Commercial invoice**
- made out by the **beneficiary**, normally in the **applicant's name**
- goods described **exactly as in the credit**
- shows the **order or contract number** and the **credit number**
- **value not above the credit amount**
- states the **terms of sale** (FOB, C&F, CIF) and shipping particulars

payload.title: The bill of lading, line by line
payload.core_explanation_md:
The bill of lading is the **receipt** from the carrier that the goods were shipped on a named vessel on a stated date. A checker confirms:

1. **Full set** of negotiable originals, as the credit requires.
2. **Signed** by the shipowner or its authorised agent.
3. **Goods description** matches the credit and the invoice.
4. **Credit number** and **issuing bank** shown.
5. **Freight** shown as paid or to pay, as the credit requires.
6. **"Shipped on board"** wording if the credit asks.
7. **Consignee**: to the **order of the shipper**, blank endorsed or endorsed to the issuing bank, as the credit says.
8. **Shipment date** inside the shipment period.
9. **Partial shipment or transhipment** noted if allowed.
10. **Not claused**, unless claused bills are allowed.

self_check.prompt_text: A bill of lading shows the goods "damaged in transit" and the credit does not allow claused bills. Which item on the checklist fails?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Item 10: a bill of lading that carries a clause about the goods' condition is claused and is not acceptable unless the credit permits it.

payload.title: The insurance document: five facts that cause most discrepancies
payload.core_explanation_md:
- **Who issues it**: the **insurance company or its agents**, signed.
- **When it starts**: dated **on or before shipment**, or showing cover effective **from the date of shipment**.
- **How much**: in the **credit's currency** and, unless the credit says otherwise, **110% of the CIF or CIP value**.
- **What it covers**: the **voyage**, naming the point where cover ends.
- **Where claims are paid**: in the **applicant's country**, **blank endorsed**, with the goods described as in the credit.

Note: the courseware cites the numbering of an older edition of the rules for these points. Under UCP 600 the insurance rules are in **Article 28**.

payload.title: The supporting documents must agree with each other
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Certificate of origin**: issued and signed by an **independent authority** such as a **Chamber of Commerce**, with the value, invoice number and bill of lading number, **consistent** with the other documents.

**Packing list, weight list, phytosanitary certificate, beneficiary's certificate and the rest**: made out **as the credit requires**.

The test across all documents is **consistency**: the same goods, quantity, weight, marks and values wherever they appear. A set that disagrees with itself invites a refusal even if each document looks fine alone.

payload.title: After the bank pays: proof that the goods actually arrived
payload.core_explanation_md:
When a bank remits foreign exchange for an import, the Reserve Bank expects **evidence that the goods came in**. For **every import**, whatever the value, the authorised dealer must make sure the importer provides it.

- **Normal imports**: the **bill of entry number, port code and date**, which the bank uses to mark evidence of import in the **IDPMS** (the import data system).
- **By post**: a **customs assessment certificate** or **postal appraisal form**; **by courier**: the **courier bill of entry**.
- **Bonded or special zones**: the **ex-bond bill of entry** or similar document.
- **Delivery against acceptance**: the bank checks the evidence in **IDPMS when it remits**. If the importer genuinely cannot show it (for example the goods are delayed), the bank may allow **reasonable time of up to three months from the date of remittance**.
- The bank creates an **Outward Remittance Message (ORM)** for every remittance.

Watch the date: RBI issued new consolidated directions on **16 January 2026**, in force from **1 October 2026**, that supersede the Import Master Direction.

payload.title: Safeguards when a bank opens credits for importers
payload.core_explanation_md:
The bank issuing a credit is on the hook for the importer. The safeguards are mostly about **knowing the customer and the supplier**.

- **Know the importer**: clear internal guidelines, due diligence and KYC, a track record; extra care on **large-value** deals or a **sudden jump in business**, and even where the importer offers **100% cash margin**.
- **Know the supplier**: a **credit report on the overseas seller**. When the bank takes documents directly from the supplier, the report may be skipped only where the invoice is **USD 300,000 or less** and the bank is satisfied about the transaction and the importer.
- **Know the rules**: exchange control, trade control, licences, delegated powers.
- **Follow up**: evidence of import; for a **sight bill** the importer does not retire, **take possession of the goods and keep insurance running**.
- **Usance credits**: only for **reputed clients** with **adequate security**, because the goods are delivered on acceptance.

payload.title: Risks in credit transactions, seen from each side
payload.core_explanation_md:
**What can go wrong for everyone**: documents **rejected for discrepancies**; local law that **conflicts** with the rules; **embargoes** or **currency restrictions**; a **court order** stopping payment even after acceptance; the buyer refusing to take up documents until the **goods arrive**; **disputes over quality** after the documents are accepted.

**For the bank**: open credits only for **regular customers**; call for bills of lading **in the bank's name**; no credits for **restricted-list goods**, and obtain the **import licence** where one is needed; apply the same checks as for **fund-based** limits even if cash margin is offered; **hedge large transactions** by a forward contract.

**For the buyer**: check the seller's **creditworthiness**; put **safety clauses** in the credit; know the **seller's country's** export rules.

**For the seller**: prepare documents **exactly** as the credit asks, so the issuing bank has **nothing to point to**.

payload.title: Two quick checks on a CIF credit: the invoice value and the insurance amount
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a credit for USD 200,000 on CIF terms asks for a commercial invoice and an insurance document in the credit's currency, with insurance as the credit says nothing more about the amount. The beneficiary presents an invoice for USD 198,500 and an insurance certificate for USD 215,000. Do the two documents pass these two checks?

worked_steps.description: Invoice value must not exceed the credit amount.
Minimum insurance amount: 110% of the CIF value of the invoice.
Compare the insured amount with the minimum.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The invoice passes, but the insurance fails: it should be at least USD 218,350.00 and is USD 3,350.00 short

self_check.prompt_text: What would the beneficiary have to do to cure the discrepancy?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Obtain a corrected insurance document for at least USD 218,350.00 and present it within the presentation period.

payload.title: Crystallising a sight import bill into rupees
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an issuing bank receives a sight import bill for USD 60,000 under a credit. The importer does not retire it within the bank's stipulated period. The bill selling rate on the crystallisation day is ₹84.2250 per USD. What rupee amount is debited to the importer, and what happens if a forward contract had been booked at ₹83.9000?

worked_steps.description: With no forward contract, convert at the bill selling rate.
With a forward contract booked, convert at the contract rate instead.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: ₹50,53,500.00 at the bill selling rate; ₹50,34,000.00 at the forward contract rate, ₹19,500.00 lower

self_check.prompt_text: For a usance bill, on what date is the liability crystallised?
self_check.expected_takeaway: On the due date of the bill.

payload.stem_md: Who draws the bill of exchange under a documentary credit, and on whom?

options.text_md: The beneficiary, on the issuing bank
options.explanation_md: This is the arrangement stated.

options.text_md: The applicant, on the advising bank
options.explanation_md: The applicant does not draw the bill.

options.text_md: The issuing bank, on the beneficiary
options.explanation_md: The bill is drawn on the bank, not by it.

options.text_md: The negotiating bank, on the applicant
options.explanation_md: The negotiating bank does not draw the bill.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The bill of exchange is drawn by the beneficiary on the issuing bank, payable at the tenor in the credit.

payload.stem_md: A credit is for USD 150,000. Which commercial invoice complies with the requirement on value?

options.text_md: An invoice for USD 151,200
options.explanation_md: The value exceeds the credit amount.

options.text_md: An invoice for USD 150,500
options.explanation_md: The value exceeds the credit amount.

options.text_md: An invoice for USD 160,000
options.explanation_md: The value exceeds the credit amount.

options.text_md: An invoice for USD 148,900
options.explanation_md: The value does not exceed the credit amount.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The invoice value should not exceed the credit amount, so only USD 148,900 complies.

payload.stem_md: A credit asks for a bill of lading issued "to the order of the shipper, blank endorsed". Which presentation matches?

options.text_md: A bill of lading consigned straight to the applicant by name
options.explanation_md: This is not "to the order of the shipper".

options.text_md: A bill of lading consigned to the order of the shipper and blank endorsed by the shipper
options.explanation_md: This matches the credit.

options.text_md: A bill of lading consigned to the order of the issuing bank, unendorsed
options.explanation_md: The credit asks for the shipper's order, blank endorsed.

options.text_md: A non-negotiable copy marked "copy"
options.explanation_md: The credit calls for negotiable originals.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The bill must be issued to the order of the shipper and blank endorsed, as the credit stipulates.

payload.stem_md: A CIF invoice is for USD 238,500. The credit says nothing about the insured amount. What is the minimum amount, in USD, for which the insurance document should be issued?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The default minimum is 110% of the CIF value: 238,500 × 110% = 262,350.00.

payload.stem_md: Who should issue and sign a certificate of origin?

options.text_md: The beneficiary itself
options.explanation_md: The certificate comes from an independent authority.

options.text_md: The issuing bank
options.explanation_md: The issuing bank does not certify origin.

options.text_md: An independent authority such as a Chamber of Commerce
options.explanation_md: This is the requirement stated.

options.text_md: The carrier
options.explanation_md: The carrier issues transport documents.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A certificate of origin must be issued and signed by an independent authority such as a Chamber of Commerce.

payload.stem_md: After remitting for an import, which of the following is evidence of import that the importer submits through the authorised dealer?

options.text_md: The invoice alone
options.explanation_md: The invoice does not show the goods entered India.

options.text_md: The bill of lading alone
options.explanation_md: The bill of lading shows shipment, not import.

options.text_md: A letter from the overseas supplier
options.explanation_md: A supplier's letter does not show the goods were imported.

options.text_md: The bill of entry number, port code and date, used to mark evidence in IDPMS
options.explanation_md: This is the standard evidence of import.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The importer submits the bill of entry number, port code and date to mark evidence of import in IDPMS, or the other customs evidence for post, courier and bonded imports.

payload.stem_md: For an import on delivery against acceptance, the importer genuinely cannot show evidence of import when the bill is remitted because the consignment is delayed. What may the authorised dealer do?

options.text_md: Refuse the remittance in every case
options.explanation_md: The bank may allow reasonable time.

options.text_md: Allow reasonable time, not exceeding three months from the date of remittance, if satisfied about the genuineness of the request
options.explanation_md: This is the discretion the Master Direction gives.

options.text_md: Allow unlimited time if the importer is a regular customer
options.explanation_md: The time cannot exceed three months.

options.text_md: Allow time only with prior RBI approval
options.explanation_md: The bank may allow it itself.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The bank may, if satisfied about genuineness, allow reasonable time not exceeding three months from the date of remittance for evidence of import.

payload.stem_md: A bank receives import bills directly from an overseas supplier for an invoice of USD 240,000 and is satisfied about the transaction and the importer's track record. Does it need a credit report on the overseas supplier?

options.text_md: Yes: a report is needed in every case
options.explanation_md: The exemption applies up to USD 300,000.

options.text_md: Yes: unless the invoice is below USD 100,000
options.explanation_md: The threshold is USD 300,000.

options.text_md: No: the report need not be obtained where the invoice value does not exceed USD 300,000 and the bank is satisfied
options.explanation_md: The exemption covers this invoice.

options.text_md: No: a report is never needed for direct bills
options.explanation_md: A report is needed above the threshold.

payload.correct_explanation_md: No credit report is needed on the overseas supplier where the invoice does not exceed USD 300,000 and the bank is satisfied about the transaction and the importer.

payload.stem_md: A sight import bill under a credit has not been retired by the importer. What does the courseware advise the bank to do about the goods?

options.text_md: Release the goods to the importer against a letter
options.explanation_md: That leaves the bank unprotected.

options.text_md: Cancel the credit and ignore the goods
options.explanation_md: The bank has an obligation under the credit.

options.text_md: Wait for the exporter to reclaim them
options.explanation_md: The bank must protect its position.

options.text_md: Take steps to take possession of the goods and keep insurance in force
options.explanation_md: This is the safeguard stated.

payload.correct_explanation_md: For a sight bill not retired, the bank should take measures to take possession of the goods and continue insurance cover.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is listed as a risk of letter of credit transactions?

options.text_md: A court order stopping payment even after the bank has accepted the documents
options.explanation_md: This is among the risks listed.

options.text_md: The credit being revocable at any time under UCP 600
options.explanation_md: UCP 600 removed revocable credits.

options.text_md: Banks examining goods instead of documents
options.explanation_md: Banks examine documents, not goods.

options.text_md: The beneficiary being unable to present documents because the credit has no expiry
options.explanation_md: Credits have an expiry date.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The courseware lists rejection for discrepancies, conflicts with local law, embargoes, currency restrictions, court stay orders, non-acceptance until goods arrive and disputes about quality among the risks.

payload.stem_md: For a usance import bill, when does the issuing bank crystallise the foreign currency liability into rupees, according to the courseware?

options.text_md: On the day the documents are received
options.explanation_md: That is when the clock may start for a sight bill.

options.text_md: On the due date of the bill
options.explanation_md: Usance bills are crystallised on the due date.

options.text_md: On the day of shipment
options.explanation_md: Shipment does not trigger crystallisation.

options.text_md: Seven days after acceptance
options.explanation_md: No such rule is stated.

payload.correct_explanation_md: For usance bills the foreign currency liability is crystallised into rupees on the due date.

payload.stem_md: A sight import bill for USD 60,000 is crystallised at a bill selling rate of ₹84.2250 per USD (illustrative). What rupee amount is debited to the importer?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Convert at the bill selling rate: 60,000 × 84.2250 = ₹50,53,500.00.

worked_solution_steps.description: Multiply by the bill selling rate

unresolved: Crystallisation of import bills (printed p. 108) rests on FEDAI guidelines that could not be retrieved; the crystallisation worked example, the usance-date question and the rupee numerical are drafted but held back from publication.

RBI's Directions on Export and Import of Goods and Services of 16 January 2026 come into force on 1 October 2026 and supersede the Import Master Direction; the substantive new text was not retrieved. The evidence-of-import card teaches the Master Direction as updated on 12 January 2026, which was in force at the 30 June 2026 cut-off, and says so.
The courseware cites UCP 500 article numbers for insurance documents; the items cite no article numbers for those.
The courseware's item that an insurance document must not be issued by a broker is not taught: it is tied to the old article numbering and was not checked against UCP 600.
Standby letters of credit in detail, URR 725, ISBP 745 and Incoterms 2020 are in later batches.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.

**For the bank**: open credits only for **regular customers**; call for bills of lading **in the bank's name**; no credits for **restricted-list goods**, and obtain the **import licence** where one is needed; apply the same checks as for **fund-based** limits even if cash margin is offered; **hedge large transactions** by a forward contract.

**For the buyer**: check the seller's **creditworthiness**; put **safety clauses** in the credit; know the **seller's country's** export rules.

**For the seller**: prepare documents **exactly** as the credit asks, so the issuing bank has **nothing to point to**.

items.title: Two quick checks on a CIF credit: the invoice value and the insurance amount
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a credit for USD 200,000 on CIF terms asks for a commercial invoice and an insurance document in the credit's currency, with insurance as the credit says nothing more about the amount. The beneficiary presents an invoice for USD 198,500 and an insurance certificate for USD 215,000. Do the two documents pass these two checks?

worked_steps.description: Invoice value must not exceed the credit amount.
Minimum insurance amount: 110% of the CIF value of the invoice.
Compare the insured amount with the minimum.

items.final_answer_with_unit: The invoice passes, but the insurance fails: it should be at least USD 218,350.00 and is USD 3,350.00 short

self_check.prompt_text: What would the beneficiary have to do to cure the discrepancy?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Obtain a corrected insurance document for at least USD 218,350.00 and present it within the presentation period.

items.title: Crystallising a sight import bill into rupees
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an issuing bank receives a sight import bill for USD 60,000 under a credit. The importer does not retire it within the bank's stipulated period. The bill selling rate on the crystallisation day is ₹84.2250 per USD. What rupee amount is debited to the importer, and what happens if a forward contract had been booked at ₹83.9000?

worked_steps.description: With no forward contract, convert at the bill selling rate.
With a forward contract booked, convert at the contract rate instead.

items.final_answer_with_unit: ₹50,53,500.00 at the bill selling rate; ₹50,34,000.00 at the forward contract rate, ₹19,500.00 lower

self_check.prompt_text: For a usance bill, on what date is the liability crystallised?
self_check.expected_takeaway: On the due date of the bill.
